:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: An asset has been depreciating in value for the past $10$ years at an annual, continuously-compounded rate of $6\%$. If that asset was initially worth $\$13\,500$, what is it worth now? Round your answer to the nearest dollar.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The continuously compounded growth equation is

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0e^{rt}. \end{aligned}
$$

We have an initial amount of

$$
P_0=13\,500
$$

a rate of $r=-0.06$, and a time duration of $t=10$ years. Substituting these values into the formula, we get

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0e^{rt} \\ &= 13\,500e^{(-0.06)(10)} \\[3pt] &= 13\,500e^{-0.6} \\[3pt] &= 13\,500(0.548\,81...) \\[3pt] &\approx 7\,409. \end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, after $10$ years, the value of the asset has decreased to $\$7\,409$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
In the year $2009$, there were approximately $4120$ crimes in a particular city. The police department then promised a $3.81 \mathrm{\% }$ annual *decrease* in crime, continuously compounded. According to this model, how many crimes occurred in $2016$? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

> A scientific calculator is required to answer this question.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The continuously compounded growth equation is $P=P_0e^{rt}$. Here $P_0=4120$, $r=-0.0381$ per year, and $t=2016-2009=7$ years. Substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= 4120e^{(-0.0381)(7)} \\
&= 4120e^{-0.2667} \\
&\approx 3155.5196.
\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer gives approximately $3156$ crimes in $2016$.

:knowledge-point/questions.:question/problem:
In medieval times, there were $9830$ people living in a city struck by a plague. If the disease resulted in a daily *decrease* in the population at a continuously compounded rate of $18 \mathrm{\% } ,$ what was the city's population after $2$ weeks? Round your answer to the nearest integer.

> A scientific calculator is required to answer this question.
:knowledge-point/questions.:question/worked-solution:
The continuously compounded growth equation is $P=P_0e^{rt}$. Here $P_0=9830$ and $r=-0.18$ per day. Convert $2$ weeks to $t=14$ days, then substitute:

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= 9830e^{(-0.18)(14)} \\
&= 9830e^{-2.52} \\
&\approx 790.9179.
\end{aligned}
$$

Rounding to the nearest integer gives approximately $791$ people.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: In a lab, a certain type of bacteria grows at a continuous rate of $5.2\%$ per day. If, after $2$ weeks, the number of bacteria is $20\,500$, what was the initial number of bacteria $2$ weeks ago? Round your answer to the nearest whole number.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The continuously compounded growth equation is

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0e^{rt}. \end{aligned}
$$

We have a final amount of $P=20\,500$, a rate of $r=0.052$, and a time duration of $t=14$ days. Substituting these values into the formula and solving for $P_0$, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= P_{0}e^{rt} \\
20500 &= P_{0}e^{(0.052)(14)} \\
20500 &= P_{0}e^{0.728} \\
20500 &= P_{0}(2.07093...) \\
P_{0} &= \frac{20500}{2.07093...} \\
P_{0} &\approx 9899
\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, there were $9\,899$ bacteria initially.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Nine years ago, an organization had $4\,350$ members. Today it has $7\,210$ members. What was its continuously compounded rate of growth during this nine-year period? Round your answer to $1$ decimal place.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The continuously compounded growth equation is

$$
P = P_0e^{rt}
$$

We have an initial amount of $P_0=4\,350$, a final amount of $P=7\,210$, and a time duration of $t=9$ years. Substituting these values into the formula and solving for $r$, we get

$$
{\begin{array}{rl}\displaystyle P & \displaystyle  = {P}_{0} {e}^{r t} \\ \displaystyle 7 \hspace{0.167em} 210 & \displaystyle  = ( 4 \hspace{0.167em} 350 ) {e}^{r ( 9 )} \\ \displaystyle {e}^{9 r} & \displaystyle  = {\displaystyle \frac{7 \hspace{0.167em} 210}{4 \hspace{0.167em} 350}} \\ \displaystyle {e}^{9 r} & \displaystyle  = 1.657 \hspace{0.167em} 47. . . \\ \displaystyle \ln   ( {e}^{9 r} ) & \displaystyle  = \ln   ( 1.657 \hspace{0.167em} 47. . . ) \\ \displaystyle 9 r & \displaystyle  = 0.505 \hspace{0.167em} 29. . . \\ \displaystyle r & \displaystyle  = 0.056 \hspace{0.167em} 14. . . \approx  5.6 \mathrm{\% } .\end{array}}
$$

Therefore, continuously compounded rate of growth is $5.6\%$.

:topic/knowledge-points.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating a Final Amount After Continuous Compounding Is Applied

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
Suppose that some money $P_0$ is deposited into a bank account. We know the bank balance $P$ after $t$ years is given by the formula

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0\left(1 + \dfrac r n \right)^{nt}, \end{aligned}
$$

where $r$ is the annual interest rate, and $n$ is the number of times payments are compounded per year.

Now suppose that we increase the number of compounding periods per year so that compounding occurs *at every instant.* We call this **continuous compounding.** When continuous compounding occurs, we can determine the balance $P$ at time $t$ using the **continuously compounded growth equation**, given by

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0e^{rt}, \end{aligned}
$$

where

$$
e\approx 2.718
$$

is Euler's number. We'll go into a little more detail regarding where this formula comes from at the end of the lesson.

For example, suppose that a company has $\$450\,000$ in the bank and that the balance grows at an annual rate of $4.5\%$, continuously compounded. Then, to calculate the bank balance $5$ years from now, we can use the continuously compounded growth equation.

In this situation, we have an initial balance

$$
P_0= 450\,000
$$

a growth rate of

$$
r= 4.5\% = 0.045
$$

and $t=5$ years. Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0e^{rt} \\[3pt] &= (450\,000)e^{(0.045)(5)} \\[3pt] &= (450\,000)e^{0.225} \\[3pt] &= (450\,000)(1.252\,322\,716) \\[3pt] &\approx 563\,545. \end{aligned}
$$

So, the balance in $5$ years will be approximately $\$563\,545$.

The rate $r$ in the continuously compounded growth equation does not have to be an annual rate. It can be over any amount of time. The time $t$ inherits its unit from the rate.

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating a Final Amount After Continuous Compounding Is Applied

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The formula for continuously compounded growth, given by

$$
P=P_0 e^{rt}
$$

is actually equal to the compound interest equation

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0 \left(1 + \dfrac r n \right)^{nt}, \end{aligned}
$$

for extremely large $n$ (in other words, as $n \rightarrow \infty$).

To demonstrate, let's take the case of $P_0=1$, $r=1$, and $t=1$. Then the formula for continuously compounded growth gives

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= P_{0}e^{1 \cdot 1} \\
&= 1e^{1 \cdot 1} \\
&= e \\
&= 2.7182818…
\end{aligned}
$$

and the compound interest equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= P_{0}(1 + \frac{r}{n})^{nt} \\
&= 1(1 + \frac{1}{n})^{n \cdot 1} \\
&= (1 + \frac{1}{n})^{n}
\end{aligned}
$$

If we substitute a large value of $n$, say

$$
n=1\,000\,000
$$

then we get

$$
\begin{aligned}
P &= (1 + \frac{1}{1000000})^{1000000} \\
&= (1.000001)^{1000000} \\
&\approx 2.718280 \\
&\approx e
\end{aligned}
$$

This result matches up nicely with our result from the formula for continuously compounded growth!

Here, we demonstrated that the result holds for the special case where $P_0=r=t=1$. However, it is possible to show that the formula is always true.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Rebecca invested $\$10,000$ into an account paying a $3\%$ annual interest, compounded monthly. How much money will be in her account after $10$ years? Round your answer to the nearest dollar.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The compound interest equation states that

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0\left(1 + \dfrac r n \right)^{nt}. \end{aligned}
$$

There are $12$ months in one year, so $n=12$. We also have an initial amount of $P_0=10,000$, an annual interest of $r=0.03$, and a length of $t=10$ years. Substituting these values into the formula, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0\left(1 + \dfrac {r} {n} \right)^{(n)(t)} \\[5pt] &= 10,000\left(1 + \dfrac {0.03} {12} \right)^{(12)(10)} \\[5pt] &= 10,000(1 + 0.0025)^{120} \\[5pt] &= 10,000(1.0025)^{120} \\[5pt] &= 10,000(1.349\,353...) \\[5pt] &= 13,493.53... \\[5pt] &\approx 13,494. \end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, after $10$ years Rebecca will have $\$13,494$ in the account.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: How much money would you need to deposit today at a $2\%$ annual interest rate, compounded yearly, to have $\$10,000$ in the account after $10$ years? Round your answer to the nearest dollar.
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The compound interest equation states that

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0\left(1 + \dfrac r n \right)^{nt}. \end{aligned}
$$

Since the payments are compounded yearly, we have $n=1$. We also have an annual rate of $r=0.02$, and a final amount of $P=10,000$ after $t=10$ years. To find the initial deposit, $P_0$, we substitute these values into the formula and solve for $P_0$:

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0\left(1 + \dfrac {r} {n}\right)^{nt} \\[5pt] 10,000 &=P_0\left(1 + \dfrac {0.02} {1}\right)^{(1)(10)} \\[5pt] 10,000 &= P_0(1.02)^{10} \\[5pt] 10,000 &= P_0(1.218,994...) \\[5pt] P_0 &= \dfrac {10,000} {1.218,994...} \\[5pt] P_0 &= 8,203.48... \\[5pt] P_0 &\approx 8,203 \end{aligned}
$$

Consequently, you would need to deposit $\$8,203$.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: If you deposit $\$4,000$ dollars into an account with a $6\%$ annual interest rate, compounded quarterly, how many years will it take until there is at least $\$8,000$ in the account?
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The compound interest equation states that

$$
\begin{aligned} P &= P_0\left(1 + \dfrac r n \right)^{nt}. \end{aligned}
$$

The annual interest is compounded quarterly, and there are $4$ quarters in one year, so $n=4$. We also have an initial amount of $P_0=4,000$ and annual rate of $r=0.06$.

To find the number of years it will take until

$$
P\geq 8,000
$$

we substitute these values into the formula and solve for $t$:

$$
\begin{aligned} P = P_0\left(1 + \dfrac r n \right)^{nt} &\geq 8,000 \\[5pt] 4,000\left(1 + \dfrac {0.06} {4} \right)^{4t} &\geq 8,000 \\[5pt] (1 + 0.015)^{4t} &\geq \dfrac {8,000} {4,000} \\[5pt] 1.015^{4t} &\geq 2 \\[5pt] \log \left(1.015^{4t}\right) &\geq \log 2 \\[5pt] 4t\log 1.015 &\geq \log 2 \\[5pt] 4t &\geq \dfrac {\log 2} {\log 1.015} \\[5pt] 4t &\geq 46.56... \\[5pt] t &\geq \dfrac{46.56...}{4} \approx 11.64 \end{aligned}
$$

Remember payments are compounded quarterly, so we must choose either $11.5$ or $11.75$ years.

- After $11.5$ years, there is still less than $\$8,000$ in the account, because $11.5<11.64$.
- After $11.75$ years, there will be more than $\$8,000$ in the account, since $11.75>11.64$.

Therefore, it will take $11.75$ years ($11$ years and $3$ quarters) until there is at least $\$8,000$ in the account.
